paper_metadata.title: Dynamic Functional Connectivity in Pediatric Mild Traumatic Brain Injury

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study utilized a large, consecutively recruited sample with clearly defined inclusion/exclusion criteria and well-matched controls. The baseline characteristics are thoroughly described, and the sample size is robust for this field.

items.label: Source of target population
items.prompt: The source population or population of interest is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: 208 patients with pmTBI (aged 8-18 years) were consecutively recruited from local Emergency Departments and Urgent Care clinics.
items.reasoning: The authors specify the age range and the clinical settings (ED/Urgent Care) which defines the target population of acute pediatric concussion.

items.label: Method used to identify population
items.prompt: The sampling frame and recruitment are adequately described, including methods to identify the sample sufficient to limit potential bias (number and type used, e.g., referral patterns in health care)
items.evidence_snippet: consecutively recruited from local Emergency Departments and Urgent Care clinics.
items.reasoning: Consecutive recruitment is the gold standard for limiting selection bias in prognosis studies.

items.label: Recruitment period
items.prompt: Period of recruitment is adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: Between July 2016 and April 2020
items.reasoning: The dates are explicitly provided.

items.label: Place of recruitment
items.prompt: Place of recruitment (setting and geographic location)  are adequately described
items.evidence_snippet: local Emergency Departments and Urgent Care clinics... University of New Mexico School of Medicine
items.reasoning: The setting and general geographic area (Albuquerque, NM via affiliations) are clear.

items.label: Inclusion and exclusion criteria
items.prompt: Inclusion and exclusion criteria are adequately described (e.g., including explicit diagnostic criteria or “zero time” description).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria consisted of a combination of the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine for mTBI (upper injury limit; Kay et al., 1993) and the Zurich Concussion in Sport Group criteria (lower injury limit; McCrory et al., 2009).
items.reasoning: The study uses validated clinical criteria and provides a detailed list of exclusions (neurologic disorders, substance abuse, etc.).

items.label: Adequate study participation
items.prompt: There is adequate participation in the study by eligible individuals
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: While the final sample size is large, the text does not explicitly state the total number of eligible individuals who declined to participate (the 'denominator' for the initial recruitment phase).

items.label: Baseline characteristics
items.prompt: The baseline study sample (i.e., individuals entering the study) is adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Table 1 lists all data for self-reported clinical outcomes and neuropsychological measures... Supplementary Table 2 [referenced for demographics].
items.reasoning: Extensive baseline data including age, sex, symptom severity, and cognitive scores are provided.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The study reports high retention rates (81-94%) and provides a clear accounting of reasons for loss to follow-up. The use of GEE/Mixed models further mitigates the impact of missing data.

items.label: Proportion of baseline sample available for analysis
items.prompt: Response rate (i.e., proportion of study sample completing the study and providing outcome data) is adequate.
items.evidence_snippet: we had excellent (pmTBI: 81%; HC: 94%) retention rates.
items.reasoning: Retention rates above 80% are generally considered low risk for attrition bias.

items.label: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out
items.prompt: Attempts to collect information on participants who dropped out of the study are described.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper lists reasons for dropout but does not describe specific attempts to collect data from those who left the study.

items.label: Reasons and potential impact of subjects lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Reasons for loss to follow-up are provided.
items.evidence_snippet: exclusions due to attrition, a lack of MRI data due to scanner upgrades, new psychological diagnosis, new MRI contraindications, the COVID-19 pandemic, positive drug tests or other reasons.
items.reasoning: A comprehensive list of reasons for attrition is provided.

items.label: Outcome and prognostic factor information on those lost to follow-up
items.prompt: Participants lost to follow-up are adequately described for key characteristics (LIST).
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: The paper does not provide a comparison table between those who completed the study and those lost to follow-up.

items.prompt: There are no important differences between key characteristics (LIST) and outcomes in participants who completed the study and those who did not.
items.evidence_snippet: Not found in text
items.reasoning: Without a comparison of completers vs. non-completers, it is impossible to definitively rule out informative censoring.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Attrition Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Loss to follow-up (from baseline sample to study population analyzed) is not associated with key characteristics (i.e., the study data adequately represent the sample) sufficient to limit potential bias to the observed relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The prognostic factor (pmTBI diagnosis) is based on international consensus criteria. The imaging methods (rs-fMRI) are highly standardized and objective.

items.label: Definition of the PF
items.prompt: A clear definition or description of 'PF' is provided (e.g., including dose, level, duration of exposure, and clear specification of the method of measurement).
items.evidence_snippet: Inclusion criteria consisted of a combination of the American Congress of Rehabilitation Medicine for mTBI... and the Zurich Concussion in Sport Group criteria
items.reasoning: The 'exposure' (pmTBI) is defined by validated clinical standards.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of PF
items.prompt: Method of PF measurement is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: Patients were examined in the sub-acute (SA; 7.4±2.2 days) and early chronic (EC; 130.9±14.5 days) stages post-injury.
items.reasoning: The timing of measurement is precise, and the diagnosis is based on clinical examination rather than just self-report.

items.prompt: Continuous variables are reported or appropriate cut-points (i.e., not data-dependent) are used.
items.evidence_snippet: The primary analyses were focused on the two local minima (k=5 and k=10)
items.reasoning: The authors used cluster validity indices (Davies-Bouldin and Ray-Turi) to determine cut-points for the dynamic states rather than arbitrary selection.

items.label: Method and Setting of PF Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of measurement of PF is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: A 3T Siemens Tim Trio scanner with a 32-channel head coil was used for image acquisition
items.reasoning: All participants underwent the same imaging protocol on the same equipment.

items.label: Proportion of data on PF available for analysis
items.prompt: Adequate proportion of the study sample has complete data for PF variable.
items.evidence_snippet: final sample consisted of 200 pmTBI and 179 HC at the SA visit
items.reasoning: The vast majority of the recruited sample provided usable data.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods of imputation are used for missing 'PF' data.
items.evidence_snippet: generalized estimating equations (GEE)... with inclusion of mean FD as nuisance covariate and random subject intercepts
items.reasoning: GEE and mixed models are appropriate for handling longitudinal data with some missingness without requiring simple imputation.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: PF Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: PF is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: Outcomes include both objective neuroimaging metrics and validated clinical scales (PCSI, PROMIS). The use of standardized software (AFNI, FSL) for imaging outcomes limits measurement bias.

items.label: Definition of the Outcome
items.prompt: A clear definition of outcome is provided, including duration of follow-up and level and extent of the outcome construct.
items.evidence_snippet: fractional occupancy (defined as the number of time points assigned to a certain state divided by the total number of time points...)
items.reasoning: The primary imaging outcomes (dFC measures) are mathematically defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Outcome
items.prompt: The method of outcome measurement used is adequately valid and reliable to limit misclassification bias (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and confirmation of outcome with valid and reliable test).
items.evidence_snippet: Functional images were preprocessed using the Analyses of Functional Neuroimages (AFNI) and FMRIB Software Library (FSL) software.
items.reasoning: The study uses industry-standard, validated software for outcome measurement.

items.label: Method and Setting of Outcome Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of outcome measurement is the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Intervals between visits were kept consistent for both groups to account for typical neurodevelopment and repeat scanning effects.
items.reasoning: The timing and environment of outcome measurement were standardized across groups.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Outcome Measurement Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Outcome of interest is adequately measured in study participants to sufficiently limit potential bias.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: While the authors adjusted for age, sex, and motion (FD), and matched the control group, there are significant baseline differences in premorbid reading and parental distress that may influence recovery trajectories and were not consistently included in all imaging models.

items.label: Important Confounders Measured
items.prompt: All important confounders, including treatments (key variables in conceptual model: LIST), are measured.
items.evidence_snippet: age-at-injury (in months) and (if available) retrospective ratings were included as covariates... mean FD as nuisance covariate
items.reasoning: Key biological and technical confounders (age, motion) were measured, but treatment/rehabilitation interventions during the 4-month window were not detailed.

items.label: Definition of the confounding factor
items.prompt: Clear definitions of the important confounders measured are provided (e.g., including dose, level, and duration of exposures).
items.evidence_snippet: mean FD higher than three times the interquartile range... age-at-injury (in months)
items.reasoning: Confounders like head motion and age are precisely defined.

items.label: Valid and Reliable Measurement of Confounders
items.prompt: Measurement of all important confounders is adequately valid and reliable (e.g., may include relevant outside sources of information on measurement properties, also characteristics, such as blind measurement and limited reliance on recall).
items.evidence_snippet: six motion parameters, their derivatives, the average white matter and cerebrospinal fluid signals
items.reasoning: Motion confounders are measured objectively via the MRI data itself.

items.label: Method and Setting of Confounding Measurement
items.prompt: The method and setting of confounding measurement are the same for all study participants.
items.evidence_snippet: Intervals between visits were kept consistent for both groups
items.reasoning: The protocol for measuring confounders was identical for patients and controls.

items.label: Method used for missing data
items.prompt: Appropriate methods are used if imputation is used for missing confounder data.
items.evidence_snippet: generalized linear mixed effects model... with inclusion of mean FD as nuisance covariate
items.reasoning: Mixed models handle missing data appropriately in the context of covariates.

items.label: Appropriate Accounting for Confounding
items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the study design (e.g., matching for key variables, stratification, or initial assembly of comparable groups).
items.evidence_snippet: age- and sex-matched group of 181 HC
items.reasoning: The study used a matched control group design.

items.prompt: Important potential confounders are accounted for in the analysis (i.e., appropriate adjustment).
items.reasoning: While age and motion were adjusted, the authors noted significant group differences in 'premorbid reading ability' and 'parental distress' which were not included in the primary imaging models.
items.evidence_snippet: significant group differences in premorbid reading ability... and effort... which formed the rationale for including these variables as covariates in the analyses of neuropsychological data [but not explicitly imaging].

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Study Confounding Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: Important potential confounders are appropriately accounted for, limiting potential bias with respect to the relationship between PF and outcome.

quips_assessment.risk_reasoning: The statistical approach is sophisticated, using LEiDA for dynamics and GEE/Mixed models for longitudinal analysis. Multiple comparison corrections (Bonferroni and Storey's FDR) were strictly applied.

items.label: Presentation of analytical strategy
items.prompt: There is sufficient presentation of data to assess the adequacy of the analysis.
items.evidence_snippet: Dynamic FC analyses were performed using the Leading Eigenvector Dynamics Analysis (LEiDA) software... k-means clustering (with cityblock [a.k.a. Manhattan] distance, 42 replicates...)
items.reasoning: The analytical pipeline is described in high detail, allowing for reproducibility.

items.label: Model development strategy
items.prompt: The strategy for model building (i.e., inclusion of variables in the statistical model) is appropriate and is based on a conceptual framework or model.
items.evidence_snippet: The primary analyses were focused on the two local minima (k=5 and k=10)... p-values for brain state-specific measures were considered statistically significant at a Bonferroni corrected α
items.reasoning: The model building was driven by data-driven cluster indices and pre-specified significance thresholds.

items.prompt: The selected statistical model is adequate for the design of the study.
items.evidence_snippet: generalized linear mixed effects model... with inclusion of mean FD as nuisance covariate and random subject intercepts
items.reasoning: Mixed effects models are the appropriate choice for longitudinal neuroimaging data.

items.label: Reporting of results
items.prompt: There is no selective reporting of results.
items.evidence_snippet: we also performed analyses for the entire range of k (3:15)... which shows the robustness of this finding
items.reasoning: The authors reported both significant and non-significant results (e.g., no relationship with symptoms) and provided sensitivity analyses across different cluster numbers.

risk_of_bias_assessment.label: Statistical Analysis and Presentation Summary
risk_of_bias_assessment.prompt: The statistical analysis is appropriate for the design of the study, limiting potential for presentation of invalid or spurious results.
